I bought the kettle on a Tuesday. This matters less than you think, but I remember it, and memory is the only instrument I have for this kind of thing.

The shop was closing. The man behind the counter had the look of someone who has sold a great many kettles and expects to sell a great many more, none of them to people he will remember. He wrapped it in newspaper. I did not ask him to. He did it anyway, with the small care of a person folding a flag, and I left feeling that I had been handed something heavier than a kettle.

Here is what I believe about objects. They do not hold memories; we lend memories to them, and then we forget we made the loan. The kettle is not sad. I am sad near the kettle. The difference is small and it is everything.

My mother kept a tin of buttons for forty years. Nobody sewed. Nobody, as far as I could tell, had ever sewn in our family, not once, not in an emergency, not even the year my father tore his only good jacket at a wedding and wore it torn for the rest of the evening with the dignity of a wounded general. Still, the tin stayed. It moved house with us three times. When she died I opened it expecting to cry and instead I laughed, because there on top, alone, was a button from that jacket.

She had kept it. Of course she had.

So I distrust people who tell me to declutter my life. I understand the argument. Fewer things, fewer burdens, more light in the room. But a room full of light is also a room where nothing has happened. I would rather live in a room where something has happened, even if I have to step around it.

The kettle, by the way, is terrible. It whistles in a key that no human song has ever used. It takes eleven minutes to boil. I have timed it. I timed it on the first morning, out of curiosity, and on the second morning out of disbelief, and on the third I stopped timing and started waiting, which is a different activity altogether and one I recommend.

Waiting, it turns out, is where the thinking happens. Not the useful thinking. The other kind. The kind that notices the light moving across the floor and wonders, without any urgency, whether the floor minds.

I am not saying the kettle made me a better person. I am saying it made me slower, and slowness is the closest thing I know to attention. You cannot love what you do not notice. You cannot notice at speed.

People ask why I do not simply buy a new one. They are right, in the way that people who ask sensible questions are always right. A new kettle would boil in three minutes. It would whistle in a reasonable key. It would come wrapped in cardboard, not in newspaper, and no man with a flag-folder's hands would hand it to me as the shop lights went out.

I will keep the terrible kettle. Not because it is good. Because it is mine, and because somewhere in its eleven minutes there is room for a button, a jacket, a wedding, and a woman who never sewed and kept everything anyway.
